Bakemeats
BAKE-meets
noun
A compound of bake and meat in its old English sense of food generally (not flesh only); hence baked provisions, pastry-work, the whole craft of the oven. The margin renders the Hebrew “the work of a baker.”

Biblical Definition

Bakemeats are baked provisions — the pastry and bread-work of a royal kitchen. The word occurs once in Scripture, and it occurs in a dream that ends at a gallows. Joseph, forgotten in the prison house, has just given the chief butler a word of restoration; the chief baker, seeing the interpretation was good, hurries to tell his own dream (Gen 40:16). He had carried three white baskets on his head, “and in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head” (Gen 40:17). Every detail damns him. The baskets are three days. The bakemeats are his office, still borne, still fine, still meant for the king’s table — and the birds are eating them off his head while he stands helpless. Joseph does not soften it: “Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee” (Gen 40:19). Three days later Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, exactly as Joseph had said (Gen 40:22). Two men dream in one night; one is restored and one is executed; the same servant of God speaks the truth to both. The bakemeats teach that a man may be full of the finest work of his hands and still be under sentence, and that the word of God distinguishes between men whom the world cannot tell apart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Baked provisions; pastry and bread-work — the whole product of the oven.

expand to see more

BAKEMEATS, meats or provisions prepared in the oven; baked goods; pastry.

From bake + meat, the older English word for food of any kind.

The AV margin glosses it “the work of a baker, or, cook.”

A KJV hapax, occurring only in the chief baker’s dream (Gen 40:17).

It names the finest output of a royal kitchen, borne in the uppermost basket.

Key Scripture

Gen 40:17 — "And in the uppermost basket there was of all manner of bakemeats for Pharaoh; and the birds did eat them out of the basket upon my head."

Gen 40:16 — "When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said unto Joseph, I also was in my dream, and, behold, I had three white baskets on my head:"

Gen 40:19 — "Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee."

Gen 40:22 — "But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them."

Modern Corruption

The prison-house chapter is flattened into a tale of a bright young man who kept a good attitude until his luck turned.

expand to see more

The live misuse of this passage is moralism. Joseph in the prison has become the property of the motivational shelf: keep your outlook high, serve where you are planted, interpret opportunity, and one day you will stand before Pharaoh. But Genesis 40 is not about Joseph’s attitude; it is about God’s revelation and God’s sentence. Joseph himself refuses the credit and names the source — do not interpretations belong to God? The chapter turns on a word from heaven given to a forgotten prisoner, by which one man is spared and another is hanged. To reduce it to a lesson in perseverance is to keep the scenery and lose the judgment, which is precisely the trade the age prefers: a Bible full of encouraging figures and empty of a God who sentences men.

The doctrine to recover is the discriminating word of God. Two officers of the same household commit the same offence, share the same cell, dream on the same night, and receive their answer from the same mouth — and the outcomes are opposite. Nothing in the baker’s conduct distinguished him from the butler; the difference lay wholly in what God had determined and revealed. So it is at the last: two women grinding at the mill, two men in one field, and the dividing word falls between them. And the sentence proved exact to the day, for the word of the LORD never fails by an hour. The bakemeats in the uppermost basket — the finest work of a condemned man’s hands, eaten by birds while he carried them — are a standing picture of every life full of accomplishment and empty of pardon.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Baked provisions — the baker’s craft, and in Scripture the emblem of a condemned man’s finest work.

expand to see more

Bakemeats — bake + meat, the old English word for food generally.

Not flesh-meat: the AV uses meat for any provision, as in meat offering.

The Hebrew margin reads “the work of a baker, or, cook.”

It appears once only, in the chief baker’s dream (Gen 40:17).

Birds devouring the bakemeats prefigured birds devouring the baker (Gen 40:19).

Usage

"The uppermost basket was full of bakemeats — and the birds were already at them."

"Bakemeats is the AV word for the oven’s work, not for flesh."

"A man may carry the finest bakemeats and still stand three days from the gallows."
